Below are the extracted atomic factual intents for chapter 5B drawn from the inspected locators of MAC-010. Each intent uses the narrowest contiguous segment range that supports it; non-contiguous material is split into separate intents. No quotation text is reproduced in semantic fields.

---

## D0001 — Mexico's macroeconomic policy framework entering the inflation surge
- chapter: 5B
- methodology_ids: 5B.3, 5B.10
- actor: Mexican macroeconomic policy authorities (Banxico, fiscal authorities)
- action: maintain prudent macroeconomic policy conduct, strong monetary and fiscal frameworks, and absence of major macroeconomic imbalances
- mechanism: institutional monetary and fiscal policy framework
- outcome: Mexico described as "well placed to navigate the challenges and risks"
- dates: described as the state of the economy entering the 2022 challenge period
- quantities: not specified beyond qualitative "strong" frameworks
- attribution: IMF Article IV staff assessment
- period_fit: 2022 H1, the year under evaluation
- limitations: forward-looking assessment with "difficult policy trade-offs" flagged
- polarity: positive (prudent frameworks cited as institutional strength)
- locator_disposition:
  - source_id: MAC-010
  - locator: page 8
  - start_segment: S00001
  - end_segment: S00004
- question_coverage: 5B.3, 5B.10
- disposition_note: narrative macro context framing for fiscal/monetary rule compliance

## D0002 — Long-standing structural obstacles to inclusive growth
- chapter: 5B
- methodology_ids: 5B.1, 5B.10
- actor: Mexican economy (pre-existing structural conditions)
- action: compound long-standing problems of low growth, weak productivity, and high inequality alongside pandemic scarring
- mechanism: structural; identified obstacles including rule of law, corruption, crime issues, regional disparities, and weak education/health outcomes
- outcome: dampened growth trajectory and weakened investment
- dates: legacy context referenced against 1999–2019 trend growth and post-pandemic period
- quantities: investment weakened during pandemic downturn (no specific figure)
- attribution: IMF Article IV staff
- period_fit: structural baseline conditioning 2022 outcomes
- limitations: aggregate framing; does not isolate the ruler's legislative agenda
- polarity: negative (named as obstacles to higher, more inclusive growth)
- locator_disposition:
  - source_id: MAC-010
  - locator: page 8
  - start_segment: S00005
  - end_segment: S00007
- question_coverage: 5B.1, 5B.10
- disposition_note: structural baseline affecting prosperity/agenda assessment

## D0003 — 2022 H1 recovery momentum and policy support
- chapter: 5B
- methodology_ids: 5B.6, 5B.9
- actor: Mexican economy (demand and fiscal policy)
- action: rebound with continued catch-up momentum, improving wages, and fiscal policy support
- mechanism: post-pandemic catch-up plus fiscal support and wage improvement
- outcome: real GDP expanded at an above-trend 1.8 percent in H1 2022; domestic demand more resilient than output; current account deficit of 0.4 percent of GDP
- dates: first half of 2022; comparison with H2 2021 stagnation
- quantities: real GDP growth 1.8 percent (above trend, H1 2022); current account deficit 0.4 percent of GDP
- attribution: IMF Article IV staff
- period_fit: directly within the year under evaluation
- limitations: H2 2021 stagnation attributed to subcontracting law and summer COVID wave (named as temporary)
- polarity: positive (recovery momentum)
- locator_disposition:
  - source_id: MAC-010
  - locator: page 8
  - start_segment: S00008
  - end_segment: S00011
- question_coverage: 5B.6, 5B.9
- disposition_note: identifies executed-budget impact and shock-response channels

## D0004 — Labor-market recovery ahead of output
- chapter: 5B
- methodology_ids: 5B.6, 5B.8
- actor: Mexican labor market
- action: improve ahead of output with steady increases in employment and decreases in un- and under-employment
- mechanism: sectoral recovery; goods-producing and some services sectors producing above pre-pandemic levels while construction and other sectors remained below
- outcome: staff-estimated output gap moved from about -2½ percent in early 2021 to nearly closed in mid-2022
- dates: past year referenced (through mid-2022); early 2021 baseline; pre-pandemic comparison
- quantities: output gap -2½ percent (early 2021); "nearly closed" (mid-2022); potential output growth temporarily below pre-pandemic rates
- attribution: IMF Article IV staff estimates
- period_fit: within 2022 evaluation window
- limitations: uneven across sectors; potential growth itself temporarily depressed
- polarity: mixed (positive labor dynamics, negative potential-growth drag)
- locator_disposition:
  - source_id: MAC-010
  - locator: page 9
  - start_segment: S00001
  - end_segment: S00004
- question_coverage: 5B.6, 5B.8
- disposition_note: labor-market and growth inputs relevant to fair distribution and infrastructure/capacity

## D0005 — Inflation trajectory and fuel-subsidy counterfactual during shock
- chapter: 5B
- methodology_ids: 5B.9
- actor: Mexican fiscal authorities
- action: increase fuel subsidies (counterfactual cited as no-subsidy benchmark)
- mechanism: fuel subsidy policy moderating energy-price inflation; counterfactual assumes no fuel subsidies but full reduction of fuel excise taxes and full pass-through to prices
- outcome: headline inflation rose from about 3 percent at end-2020 to 7.4 percent at end-2021 and 8.7 percent by August 2022; energy-price inflation moderated after initial 2021 surge; food inflation reached 14.1 percent in August and accounted for over 50 percent of above-target headline increase; core inflation rose to 8.1 percent
- dates: end-2020, end-2021, August 2022
- quantities: headline 3 → 7.4 → 8.7 percent; core 8.1 percent (August 2022); food 14.1 percent; food share of above-target headline inflation >50 percent
- attribution: IMF Article IV staff; data from EIA, Banxico, Haver Analytics
- period_fit: directly within 2022 shock period
- limitations: medium-term expectations rising notably while longer-term expectations remain broadly stable; near-term expectations above upper target limit
- polarity: mixed (shock response subsidies helped energy component; food and core inflation continued upward)
- locator_disposition:
  - source_id: MAC-010
  - locator: page 9
  - start_segment: S00005
  - end_segment: S00011
- question_coverage: 5B.9
- disposition_note: shock-response fiscal instrument and its measurable effects

## D0006 — Phillips-curve analysis attributing inflation surge to energy, food, residual pressures
- chapter: 5B
- methodology_ids: 5B.3, 5B.7
- actor: IMF staff analytical exercise
- action: estimate a hybrid Phillips curve (2003–2019 sample, excluding pandemic) and run a dynamic in-sample forecast for 2021Q1–2022Q2
- mechanism: regression of inflation on expected inflation (β≈0.52), lagged inflation (≈0.48), labor-market slack, REER, energy, food, US core CPI
- outcome: rising energy and then food prices explain much of the headline surge through 2021Q3; residual cost-push pressures contributed in 2022Q1; expected and lagged inflation weights are roughly equal for headline (0.52 vs 0.48), consistent with relatively greater role of past inflation in EMEs
- dates: estimation 2003Q1–2019Q4 (headline) and 2003Q1–2020Q4 variants; forecast 2021Q1–2022Q2
- quantities: β expectations 0.52; lagged 0.48; energy coefficient 0.16; raw food prices 0.20 (headline); unemployment gap coefficient -0.06; R² 0.75–0.77 (headline), 0.33–0.34 (core); Durbin–Watson ~2
- attribution: IMF staff calculations; Banxico for expectations
- period_fit: directly relevant to 2022 inflation episode
- limitations: results robust to alternative specifications and time-varying coefficients; pandemic period omitted due to exceptional volatility; analysis explanatory, not causal for residual components
- polarity: mixed (positive that standard determinants explain much; negative that residual pressures are large)
- locator_disposition:
  - source_id: MAC-010
  - locator: page 81
  - start_segment: S00004
  - end_segment: S00019
- question_coverage: 5B.3, 5B.7
- disposition_note: provides analytical evidence on shock drivers and monitoring/audit of inflation dynamics

## D0007 — Inflation expectations and structural food-price role
- chapter: 5B
- methodology_ids: 5B.3, 5B.9
- actor: Banxico (inflation targeting regime since 2001) and Mexican inflation dynamics
- action: register multi-decade inflation highs with food prices contributing roughly half of above-target headline inflation
- mechanism: rebound in global fuel prices (early 2021) followed by sharp goods and food price increases; above-target food-inflation episodes recurred in 2008, 2011–13, 2017–18
- outcome: inflation expectations raised near-term concerns about de-anchoring, but only near-term expectations have increased; core inflation less explained by standard determinants (R² 0.33–0.34)
- dates: surge began early 2021; multi-decade highs observed
- quantities: food contribution ≈ half of above-target headline inflation; raw food coefficient 0.20 in headline Phillips curve; core R² 0.33–0.34
- attribution: IMF staff and Banxico; Haver Analytics
- period_fit: 2022 surge, with historical context since 2001
- limitations: standard determinants explain less of core inflation; pass-through from relative-price shocks to core appears smaller pre-pandemic
- polarity: mixed (food-price pressures dominant; monetary credibility so far intact for medium/long term)
- locator_disposition:
  - source_id: MAC-010
  - locator: page 80
  - start_segment: S00001
  - end_segment: S00014
- question_coverage: 5B.3, 5B.9
- disposition_note: rule-credibility and shock-mitigation evidence

## D0008 — FSAP key recommendations on autonomy, supervision, and crisis management
- chapter: 5B
- methodology_ids: 5B.3, 5B.4, 5B.5
- actor: IMF FSAP team (recommendations to Mexican financial authorities)
- action: issue prioritized recommendations tagged by horizon (NT/MT/C) across cross-cutting, systemic risk, financial-sector oversight, financial integrity, and crisis management
- mechanism: recommendations covering autonomy of regulatory agencies, supervisory protection, Pillar 2 use, liquidity stress testing, macroprudential strategy and toolkit (LTV/DSTI), consolidated supervision, CEFER refinement, cybersecurity, climate-related guidance, AML/CFT follow-up, ELA framework, bail-in powers, and resolution planning
- outcome: structured list of pending reforms with designated implementation horizons; current text does not record execution status beyond the recommendation catalogue
- dates: publication context 2022 IMF Article IV (timing of recommendations is contemporary)
- quantities: not quantified (qualitative priority/horizon tags)
- attribution: IMF FSAP, Annex XI
- period_fit: 2022 reform agenda context
- limitations: Annex XI catalogues recommendations; status of implementation not provided in these segments
- polarity: mixed (reform agenda targets known gaps; execution status unstated in the inspected locator)
- locator_disposition:
  - source_id: MAC-010
  - locator: page 88
  - start_segment: S00001
  - end_segment: S00012
- question_coverage: 5B.3, 5B.4, 5B.5
- disposition_note: institutional rule-making and supervisory-enforcement agenda

## D0009 — Tax-administration reform agenda and revenue performance
- chapter: 5B
- methodology_ids: 5B.1, 5B.3, 5B.5
- actor: Mexican government (current administration) tax-policy authorities
- action: enact notable tax-administration reforms since 2019: abolish offset of excess tax credits across taxes; require digital-platform withholding; implement GAAR and prohibit tax-driven mergers; enact BEPS actions 2, 4, and 12
- mechanism: compliance-focused revenue mobilization, including VAT-gap analysis
- outcome: income and corporate tax and VAT revenues grew as a share of GDP (expected increases of 1.0 and 0.6 percent of GDP between 2019 and 2022); estimated VAT evasion reduction of about MEX$170 billion between 2018 and 2021; strong revenue performance attributed at least partially to compliance policy bedding-in
- dates: reforms since 2019; revenue effect measured 2019–2022; VAT evasion window 2018–2021
- quantities: +1.0 percent of GDP (income tax), +0.6 percent of GDP (corporate tax/VAT bucket as listed); MEX$170 billion VAT evasion reduction
- attribution: IMF Article IV staff; authorities' VAT-gap analysis
- period_fit: directly within 2022 evaluation period (with 2019 baseline)
- limitations: isolating impact of reforms is difficult due to successive shocks and labor-market reform effects; diminishing returns expected; new customs focus overlaps with security issues and requires army coordination
- polarity: positive (compliance reforms and revenue gains) tempered by expected diminishing returns
- locator_disposition:
  - source_id: MAC-010
  - locator: page 90
  - start_segment: S00001
  - end_segment: S00014
- question_coverage: 5B.1, 5B.3, 5B.5
- disposition_note: legislative agenda, fiscal-rule compliance, and anti-evasion enforcement

## D0010 — Pension-system reform: parameters, distributional intent, and labor-market risk
- chapter: 5B
- methodology_ids: 5B.1, 5B.6, 5B.8
- actor: Mexican government (current administration)
- action: reform the pension system since 2019, replacing the means-tested social pension with a basic pension and adjusting parameters in 2021
- mechanism: raise total contribution rates from 6.5–10 percent to 15 percent by 2030 (employer share rising to 13.875 percent for high earners; government subsidies concentrated on low earners); lower minimum years of contributions from ~25 to 15 years in 2021 (rising to 20 by 2031); introduce significantly higher minimum pensions with career-earnings differentiation; cap fees
- outcome: increased pension eligibility (some pensioners became immediately eligible for funded pensions instead of lump sums); government contributions change from 2023; employer contribution rates rise gradually to final values in 2030; minimum pension lowest bracket raised to MEX$45,000 for someone with 20 years
- dates: 2019 (means-tested replacement), 2021 (parameter reforms), 2023 (government contribution changes), 2030 (final contribution-rate targets), 2031 (minimum-years threshold)
- quantities: contribution-rate range 6.5%–10% → 15% by 2030; employer share up to 13.875% for high earners; minimum contribution years ~25 → 15 (2021) → 20 (2031); minimum pension floor MEX$45,000 for 20-year careerers; pre-2021 single minimum pension of almost MEX$40,000
- attribution: IMF Article IV staff, Annex XIII
- period_fit: 2022 reform-design context with implementation timeline stretching beyond 2022
- limitations: IMF notes reforms "might adversely affect labor market incentives and push more workers in the informal market"; transition-period effects on long-term contributors; distributional incidence between high/low earners explicit
- polarity: mixed (positive coverage and equity intent for low earners; negative potential labor-market distortion)
- locator_disposition:
  - source_id: MAC-010
  - locator: page 91
  - start_segment: S00001
  - end_segment: S00017
- question_coverage: 5B.1, 5B.6, 5B.8
- disposition_note: legislative agenda and fair-distribution lens, with explicit labor-market caveat

## D0011 — Event-study caveat on trade-diversion estimates
- chapter: 5B
- methodology_ids: 5B.7
- actor: IMF staff event-study analysis (Annex VIII)
- action: report positive trade-diversion estimates from 2014 US sanctions on Russia for Mexico's exports to the US
- mechanism: dynamic regressions and local projections using UN Comtrade HS-6-digit data, USITC tariffs, and Mexican GDP controls
- outcome: pre/post-sanction comparison shows Mexico's exports to the US rose by about USD 0.85 billion or 0.07 percentage points of 2012 GDP (comparing 2015–16 vs 2012–14); local projections suggest a statistically significant ~10 percent nominal-export increase four months after the shock
- dates: 2014 sanctions; sample 2012–2016; Annex within 2022 Article IV
- quantities: USD 0.85 billion; 0.07 percent of 2012 GDP; ~10 percent nominal-export increase at four months
- attribution: IMF staff; UN Comtrade; USITC
- period_fit: historical comparator, not 2022 outcome; used as a clue for 2022 sanctions scenario
- limitations: explicitly "does not attribute causality" because the approach could capture other time-varying effects; results only "clues" rather than direct 2022 measurement
- polarity: positive (diversion signal) tempered by explicit non-causal caveat
- locator_disposition:
  - source_id: MAC-010
  - locator: page 78
  - start_segment: S00001
  - end_segment: S00016
- question_coverage: 5B.7
- disposition_note: relevant for transparent-information and independent-evaluation lens with explicit limitations
- secondary_locator_disposition:
  - source_id: MAC-010
  - locator: page 79
  - start_segment: S00001
  - end_segment: S00002
  - rationale: non-contiguous caveat material that completes the limitation statement

## D0012 — Inflationary persistence and expectations-anchoring risk
- chapter: 5B
- methodology_ids: 5B.3, 5B.7, 5B.9
- actor: Banxico and inflation-expectations surveys
- action: monitor near-term inflation expectations that have moved above the upper limit of the target range, while medium-term expectations are "rising notably" and longer-term expectations "remain broadly stable"
- mechanism: structural feature that past price surprises (including food and supply shocks) feed into current inflation with relatively long persistence in EMEs
- outcome: persistent volatility risk; current episode differs from 2017–18 in that residual pressures are larger
- dates: 2022 Article IV publication context; multi-year Phillips-curve evidence 2003–2020
- quantities: near-term expectations above upper limit; medium-term rising notably; long-term broadly stable
- attribution: IMF Article IV narrative; Banxico survey-based expectations
- period_fit: directly within 2022 evaluation
- limitations: only near-term expectations have risen materially so far; standard determinants explain relatively less of core inflation
- polarity: mixed (rules/framework positive; expectations-anchoring risk negative)
- locator_disposition:
  - source_id: MAC-010
  - locator: page 9
  - start_segment: S00009
  - end_segment: S00010
- question_coverage: 5B.3, 5B.7, 5B.9
- disposition_note: complements D0007 with contemporaneous expectations narrative
